name: Upper Peninsula Assessment — Caldwell-Vance Trade Partners, Internal Memo Q3-2213
author: Fenella Johansson-Achebe, Director of Northern Accounts, Caldwell-Vance Trade Partners
description: An internal trading company memo assessing the economic potential of the Upper Peninsula, whose professional tone cannot conceal its unease about what their scouts found there.
body:
TO: Northern Accounts Executive Committee
FROM: Fenella Johansson-Achebe, Director of Northern Accounts
RE: Upper Peninsula Assessment, Q3-2213 Field Survey
CLASSIFICATION: Internal — Do Not Forward

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Following the Q2 directive to evaluate the Upper Peninsula as a potential new supply corridor, I am submitting this memo to recommend we table the initiative for a minimum of eighteen months and revisit with a larger team. The economic potential is real. The operational picture is not what we expected.

WHAT WE WERE TOLD TO EXPECT
The UP has approximately forty thousand permanent residents across its twelve significant communities, with the majority concentrated around Marquette, Sault Ste. Marie (the southern approach), and Houghton. Primary exports historically: copper, timber, fish. The survey was meant to assess whether those exports had recovered to tradeable levels after two centuries of minimal outside contact.

WHAT WE FOUND
The communities are real and the people are real. Marquette is larger than the population figures suggest — my field team estimated sixty to eighty thousand residents in the extended metro area, which implies either the census data is two decades old (plausible) or significant in-migration from further north that isn't being reported (also plausible, and worth noting).

Copper is present and being processed. The Keweenaw communities have maintained smelting operations continuously since the pre-Consolidation era, which is a remarkable industrial achievement given their isolation. The copper is high quality. The communities want Φ, or failing that, GLMZ-manufactured electronic components. This is a tradeable relationship if we can establish reliable transit.

Fish is present. Lake Superior is in better ecological condition than Lake Michigan — the industrial runoff history is different and the UP communities have been managing it carefully. The fishers we spoke with had opinions about sustainable harvest limits that made our team uncomfortable because the opinions were correct.

THE OPERATIONAL PICTURE
Here is where I need to be direct with the committee.

The transit situation is not good. There is no maintained road connection between the UP and GLMZ that a freight vehicle can use between November and April. The Mackinac crossing is seasonal and controlled by the Bridge Communities Authority, which is not a GLMZ-aligned entity and has its own ideas about what passage fees are appropriate. The BCA is not hostile — they are simply operating independently and have been for a long time. They will not negotiate below their standard rate and they are correct that we need them more than they need us.

The further north you go from Marquette, the less certain I am about conditions. My field team did not proceed past the Huron Mountains, and I want to be honest about why. The communities north of the Huron Mountains did not extend invitations, and our lead surveyor — Ravi Korhonen-Touré, who has worked for us for eleven years — declined to proceed without invitation. He described the communities as 'not hostile, not welcoming, and not interested in the distinction.' I have worked with Ravi for eleven years. If he said we should stop, we stopped.

What he did relay from conversations in Marquette: the northern communities have been in sustained contact with what people variously called 'the Alaska cousins' or 'the Tribe network' — cultural and kinship connections to the 13 Tribes of Alaska that appear to be active, not historical. There is transit happening between the UP and Alaska that we cannot map, by means we cannot explain given the distances involved. This is not relevant to our immediate assessment but it is notable.

ONE ADDITIONAL ITEM
I am going to include this because I think the committee deserves accurate information. Three members of my field team reported the same experience on separate nights during the northern survey: waking in the early hours with the strong sense that someone was standing outside their shelter, followed by a sound that none of them could describe consistently but which all three described as 'patient.' In the morning, on two occasions, there were marks in the ground near the shelters — not footprints, not anything I can identify from the photographs. The Marquette locals, when asked, said they did not know what made the marks and changed the subject.

I am not a superstitious person. I am reporting what my team experienced. I am recommending the eighteen-month delay.

RECOMMENDATION
Table the initiative. Reopen when we have better transit infrastructure and clearer communication with the BCA. The copper is worth it. But we go in prepared or we don't go in.
